newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ markets unsure of goalposts after Brash comment.
newsitem.headline: NZ markets unsure of goalposts after Brash comment.

text.p: New Zealand market players were generally united in their view on Friday that the central bank had shifted the goalposts for desired monetary conditions, but opinion was mixed as to how far they had been moved.

The Reserve Bank prompted a sharp easing in conditions late on Thursday when governor Don Brash said in a wire agency interview the central bank would need to review whether its assumptions on conditions were appropriate.
Brash also said it was significant that conditions had eased somewhat over the last few weeks.
The debt market read the comments as sanctioning easier monetary conditions and pushed 90-day bank bill rates below seven percent for the first time since August 1994.
The 90-days are now at 6.85 percent from 7.03 percent before the comments, while the currency's Trade Weighted Index (TWI) is at 68.45 from 68.9.
In its March economic projections the RBNZ said it preferred 90-days at 7.5 percent and a TWI at 68.0, or an equivalent mix.
"We've swung around completely now from where we were two days ago," a money market dealer told Reuters.
"Right now, the morning after the (comments), the market hasn't made an actual level, a line in the sand. But that's the next step -- to ask where are the goalposts now?"

A Wellington dealer said she agreed with the market's view that the RBNZ was signalling those assumptions were now inappropriately tight, and were likely to be changed when the bank releases its June monetary policy statement.

She suspected a TWI at 68.0 and 90-day bills at 6.6 percent was now the desired mix, adding that would give core inflation in the June 1998 year of 1.5 percent, the mid point of the RBNZ's 0-3 percent target band. Based on its March assumptions the bank has forecast June 1998 annual inflation of 0.8 percent.
"You have to ask what are they trying to achieve here? What is their purpose? And that's 1.5 percent -- it's not 0.8 percent," the dealer said.

"But personally speaking, I don't think it will trade down to 6.6 percent unless we get some reassurance from the Reserve Bank -- some people are looking, even today, for reassurance that the market is moving in the right direction."
When approached by Reuters, the RBNZ declined to comment on the appropriateness of the market's easing.
Another dealer suggested 90-days at 6.6 percent (on a TWI at 68.0 percent) was "probably a little bit low".
He questioned whether the RBNZ would be happy with further sharp falls in rates with the TWI currently around 68.50.
"There's obviously some form of an easing expected -- I guess we're going to settle into a 6.75-7.00 percent range in those 90-days until how much (of an easing) becomes clear.
"You can't really go too much further than that before you start to go overboard."

However, ANZ Bank senior manager of domestic markets Jim Reardon said that given the TWI at 68.50 the 90-days should be "easily" below 6.5 percent, and he saw them breaking below that level "sometime in the next week or so".
"If anything I suspect that what's going to happen is we're going to see a break in our market, and we may actually overshoot(desired conditions) rather than undershoot," he added.
"The currency is holding up very well... I don't for a minute believe the currency is about to fall out of bed. That being the case, there is room for rates to ease."
Dealers agreed March quarter employment data next Tuesday should help shed more light on inflation prospects and the appropriate level of monetary conditions.
